chapters.name: Signs, Signals, and Pavement Markings
chapters.summary: What sign shapes and colors mean, how to respond to steady and flashing traffic lights, and what lane lines and other pavement markings tell you. Questions here show a sign, a light, or a painted line and ask what you must do; several use pictures of yellow warning signs such as Stop Ahead, Signal Ahead, Merge, Cross Road, and Divided Highway, plus the railroad crossbuck, Keep Right, and Wrong Way.
keyPoints: Shapes with no words: 8 sides = STOP, 5 sides = school zone or crossing, downward triangle = YIELD, round yellow with X and RR = railroad ahead, sideways pennant on the left = no-passing zone.
Colors: yellow = general warning, orange = work zone, brown = parks and recreation, white with black letters = a rule such as a speed limit.
Blinking red = full stop every time, like a STOP sign. Blinking yellow = no stop needed, just slow down and take care.
No light showing at all = all-way stop for every direction, whatever the size of the road.
Shared center lane (solid plus broken yellow on both edges) = only for starting or finishing a left turn, never for passing or travel.

pitfalls.trap: When a traffic light is completely dark, drivers on the bigger road may keep going without stopping.
pitfalls.fact: Under Texas law, a signal showing no light at all is handled like an all-way stop, so you come to a full stop even on the larger road. Then take your turn when it is safe; there is no need to wait for police to arrive.

pitfalls.trap: A flashing yellow left-turn arrow means oncoming traffic must stop, so you can turn freely.
pitfalls.fact: Only a solid green arrow stops oncoming traffic for you. A flashing yellow arrow allows the left turn, but you must yield to oncoming cars and to people in the crosswalk and turn only when there is a safe gap.

pitfalls.trap: Holding your left arm out and bent upward at the elbow means you are turning left.
pitfalls.fact: Arm bent upward means a right turn. A left turn is shown with the arm held straight out, and an arm bent downward means slowing or stopping. All three Texas hand signals are given from the left side of the car, which is why the right-turn signal is easy to mix up.

chapters.name: Right of Way and Turns
chapters.summary: Who goes first at intersections, four-way stops, and roundabouts, how to make turns correctly, and when you must yield to pedestrians and emergency vehicles. Questions here describe one moment at a Texas intersection, such as two cars stopping together, a fire truck coming as you reach a corner, a pedestrian on a WALK signal, or a red light when you want to turn, and ask who must wait or what you may do.
keyPoints: Four-way stop order: first to stop goes first. On a tie, the car on the right goes and the car on the left waits. Size, speed, honking, or waving never decides it.
You are the one who waits when you turn left on a green with no arrow, enter a roundabout, merge from a freeway ramp, or leave a driveway (stop before the sidewalk).
People on foot in a crosswalk on your half of the road, or crossing on a WALK signal, go before your turning car.
Siren and flashing lights: move to the right-hand edge or curb, stay out of the intersection, and stay stopped until the vehicle has passed.
Red-light turns in Texas: right on red after a full stop unless a sign forbids it; left on red only from a one-way street onto another one-way street.
Turn signal: at least the last 100 feet before a turn. U-turn ban: curves and hilltops where other drivers cannot see you within 500 feet.

pitfalls.trap: In Texas you may turn left on red from a two-way street onto a one-way street.
pitfalls.fact: Left on red is legal in Texas only when both streets are one-way and you turn with traffic, after a full stop and yielding. Starting from a two-way street, you must wait for green, even with no traffic in sight.

pitfalls.trap: If a fire truck with its siren on comes as you reach an intersection, stopping in the middle of it keeps you out of the way.
pitfalls.fact: Texas law says to pull over parallel to and as close as possible to the right-hand edge or curb, clear of any intersection, and stop until it passes. A car stopped inside the intersection can block the fire truck if it needs to turn there.

pitfalls.trap: Blinking your left turn signal to show the driver behind you that it is safe to pass is a legal courtesy.
pitfalls.fact: Texas law does not allow using turn signals as a "go ahead and pass" signal, because only the driver behind can judge whether passing is safe. Your signals are for turning, changing lanes, or pulling away from a curb.

chapters.name: Speed, Lanes, Passing, and Parking
chapters.summary: Texas speed limits, choosing a safe speed, lane use and passing, following distance, and where you may not park. Most questions here ask for one Texas number when no sign is posted, such as the limit in an alley, on a beach, or on a numbered highway, or the parking distance from a hydrant, crosswalk, stop sign, or railroad. Others ask when you may use a paved shoulder or how to park on a one-way street.
keyPoints: Unposted Texas limits: 15 mph for an alley or beach, 30 mph for an urban district street, 60 mph for a rural road that is not a numbered highway, and 70 mph for a numbered state or U.S. highway outside town.
Rain or fog: driving at the posted number can still be illegal if it is too fast for the conditions.
No parking within: 15 ft of a fire hydrant, 20 ft of a crosswalk at an intersection, 30 ft of a stop sign or signal on the approach, 50 ft of the nearest railroad rail.
Parked at a curb: face the way traffic moves, with the curb-side wheels no more than 18 inches away (left wheels on the left side of a one-way street).
Town no-passing zone: within 100 feet of an intersection or railroad crossing, you may not use the left side of the road to pass.
Following distance: count seconds from a fixed object, not car lengths.

pitfalls.trap: Any rural Texas road with no sign posted has a 70 mph limit.
pitfalls.fact: 70 mph is the unposted limit only on U.S. or state numbered highways, including farm-to-market and ranch-to-market roads, outside an urban district. Other roads outside town, such as county roads, default to 60 mph.

pitfalls.trap: On a Texas beach with no posted limit, you may drive 25 or 30 mph, like on a city street.
pitfalls.fact: The Texas beach limit is 15 mph unless another limit is posted, the same number as an alley. 30 mph is the city street limit; the beach number is lower because people, children, and pets may be in your path.

pitfalls.trap: A wide, empty paved shoulder may be used to get around a long line of slow traffic.
pitfalls.fact: Texas allows driving on an improved shoulder only when it is necessary and safe and for listed reasons, such as passing a car that is slowing or stopped to turn left, or slowing to turn right. Skipping ahead of slow traffic is not one of them.

chapters.name: Safe Driving and Sharing the Road
chapters.summary: Driving at night and in bad weather, handling skids and emergencies, and sharing the road with school buses, trucks, motorcycles, bicycles, trains, and work zones. Questions here test Texas distances and speeds, such as when headlights must be on, when to dim high beams, where to stop at a railroad crossing, and how much to slow down for a stopped tow truck or ambulance, plus when you must stop for a school bus.
keyPoints: Headlights on: 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise, or whenever you cannot clearly see 1,000 feet ahead. In fog, low beams only.
Switch to low beams: 500 feet from an oncoming car, 300 feet behind a car you follow.

School bus with red lights flashing: stop from either direction on a road with no median; you may go on only when the bus is on the other roadway of a divided highway. First-offense fine for passing it: $500 to $1,250.
Railroad: stop 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail. Stalled on the tracks with a train coming: get everyone out before anything else.
Move Over or Slow Down: leave the lane, or slow to 20 mph under the limit (60 becomes 40). At a limit of 25 mph or less, slow to 5 mph.
Skid: lift off the gas gently and steer toward your path, no hard braking. Truck blind spot: if the driver's face is not visible in the truck's side mirror, assume you are hidden.

pitfalls.trap: On a two-lane road, you may keep going when a stopped school bus is in the opposite lane.
pitfalls.fact: On a road with no median, drivers from both directions must stop for a bus with red lights flashing, and wait until it moves, the lights go off, or the driver signals you to go. Only a bus on the other roadway of a divided highway lets you continue.

pitfalls.trap: When you come up behind another car, you may keep your high beams on until you are within 500 feet.
pitfalls.fact: The 500-foot rule is for a car coming toward you. When you follow a car, Texas requires low beams within 300 feet, because glare in its mirrors can blind the driver.

pitfalls.trap: If you cannot move over for a stopped tow truck on a 60 mph road, slowing to 50 mph is enough.
pitfalls.fact: Texas requires slowing to 20 mph below the posted limit when you cannot safely change lanes, so 60 mph becomes 40 mph. On a road posted at 25 mph or less, slow to 5 mph instead.

chapters.name: Licensing, Alcohol, and Driver Responsibility
chapters.summary: Graduated driver license rules for teens, insurance and crash duties, alcohol and drug laws, implied consent, phone use, and seat belts. Questions here ask for Texas age rules and numbers, such as the learner license age, the teen phone ban, the 0.08 and zero-tolerance alcohol limits, the 180-day refusal suspension, and 30/60/25 insurance, and what to do after hitting a parked car.
keyPoints: Teen steps: learner license at 15. The supervising driver must be 21 or older, licensed for at least 1 year, and in the front passenger seat.
First 12 months of a provisional license (under 18): no driving midnight to 5 a.m. except work, a school activity, or a medical emergency; at most one non-family passenger under 21.
Alcohol: 0.08 makes a driver 21 or older legally intoxicated. Under 21, any detectable amount is an offense (not 0.02, not 0.05).
Refusing a breath or blood test after a DWI arrest: 180-day suspension the first time, 2 years with an earlier refusal in the past 10 years.
Phones: texting banned for every driver; under 18, no wireless device at all, hands-free included, except in an emergency; in an active school crossing zone, handheld only when stopped.
Insurance minimum 30/60/25 ($30,000 / $60,000 / $25,000). Minor freeway crash, no injuries, cars drivable: move them out of the main lanes.

pitfalls.trap: A 17-year-old may take calls with a hands-free device as long as there is no texting.
pitfalls.fact: Hands-free calls are allowed for adults, but Texas bans drivers under 18 from using any wireless device while driving, even hands-free, except in an emergency. There is no exception for calls from a parent.

pitfalls.trap: A 19-year-old may drive after a beer as long as the alcohol level stays under 0.02.
pitfalls.fact: Texas has zero tolerance for drivers under 21: any detectable amount of alcohol while driving is an offense. 0.08 is the adult limit, and neither 0.02 nor 0.05 is a Texas limit for minors.

pitfalls.trap: After denting an empty parked car, a note with just your phone number is enough.
pitfalls.fact: Texas law calls for a written note left where it can be seen, giving the names and addresses of the driver and of the owner of the car that hit it, plus a short explanation. Finding the owner also works; driving away with no note is illegal.
